headline: Massachusetts report finds decades of abuse across three Catholic dioceses
dek: The attorney general's investigation found evidence that more than 270 clerics abused nearly 1,000 children and documented failures to report allegations, supervise accused priests and protect survivors.
body: Massachusetts Attorney General Andrea Joy Campbell released a long-awaited report Wednesday that found evidence more than 270 Catholic clerics abused nearly 1,000 children across the dioceses of Fall River, Springfield and Worcester. The investigation is the first comparable public accounting of abuse and institutional failures in those three dioceses, following earlier public scrutiny of the Archdiocese of Boston.

The findings cover decades of allegations, with cases dating at least to the 1950s, according to WBUR News. The attorney general's office said investigators reviewed more than 300,000 pages of records and interviewed more than 100 people, including survivors, advocates, attorneys, clergy, diocesan employees and officials. The full magnitude cannot be known, the report says, because some records were missing or unavailable, dioceses did not keep consistently organized complaint records and some survivors never reported what happened. (https://www.wbur.org/news/2026/09/30/massachusetts-attorney-general-clergy-sex-abuse-worcester-fall-river-springfield; https://www.mass.gov/doc/2026-fall-river-springfield-and-worcester-diocese-report/download)

The report describes recurring failures by church leaders before and after allegations surfaced. It says accused or offending priests were transferred to other parishes without the reasons being disclosed, some returned to ministry after treatment without adequate supervision, restrictions were not consistently enforced and the reasons for removing priests from ministry were sometimes concealed. Investigators also found that allegations were not consistently reported to law enforcement, according to the attorney general's release. Those conclusions concern institutional conduct documented by the investigation; they are not a criminal verdict against every person named in the report.

The report's release does not produce a new wave of indictments. GBH News reported that Campbell said Massachusetts law prevented prosecutors from pursuing many cases because some conduct was not criminal when it occurred or the statute of limitations had expired. Three cases were referred to district attorneys during the investigation, and one resulted in criminal charges, Campbell said. She emphasized that those legal limits do not erase the evidence or reduce the harm described by survivors.

The findings also expose an unresolved transparency divide among the dioceses. Worcester is the only Massachusetts diocese that has not published a public list of credibly accused clergy, WBUR and GBH reported. Worcester spokesperson Raymond Delisle said the diocese welcomed the report and would study it, while pointing to its own earlier reports and current screening and safety procedures. Fall River Bishop Edgar M. da Cunha said he was sorry to survivors and noted that his diocese published a list of clergy with credible allegations five years ago. Springfield did not immediately respond to WBUR's request for comment. (https://www.wgbh.org/news/local/2026-09-30/catholic-clerics-abused-nearly-1-000-children-in-springfield-worcester-fall-river-dioceses-report)

Campbell urged all three dioceses to put survivors first, investigate allegations properly, report suspected abuse, enforce restrictions on accused and offending priests and maintain transparent records. The report's recommendations matter across western and southeastern Massachusetts because the dioceses serve communities far beyond their headquarters in Springfield, Worcester and Fall River; the institution's response affects parish families, schools and any survivor deciding whether it is safe to come forward.

The attorney general also called for government action. She supports legislation that would remove or extend time limits for child-sex-abuse claims, including a possible lookback period for older cases. State Sen. Joan Lovely told WBUR that a related proposal was in a conference committee, but its path to the Legislature and governor remained unresolved. For survivors, that debate is the practical next step after the report: the investigation has created a public record, while lawmakers must decide whether Massachusetts' legal system gives people abused as children a meaningful route to accountability.
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: Massachusetts AG report details clergy abuse in three dioceses
seoDescription: A Massachusetts attorney general investigation found evidence that more than 270 Catholic clerics abused nearly 1,000 children across three dioceses.
